title: Tanker With Three Indians Hit Near Hormuz; Accounts Differ on Crew Casualties
excerpt: India's shipping minister says all three Indian seafarers and the whole crew of the MT Navig8 Messi are safe; the operator reports one crew member missing and 11 injured.
body:
• The Liberia-flagged tanker MT Navig8 Messi, carrying three Indian seafarers, was struck by a projectile in the Persian Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz.
  • India's shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal says all three Indians and the entire crew are safe and accounted for, with one Indian officer taken to hospital for first-aid treatment.
  • The vessel's operator, ADNOC Logistics & Services, reports a different toll: one crew member missing, 11 injured and the crew evacuated, with search and rescue under way. The two accounts had not been reconciled.
  • The strike comes two days after the LPG tanker Tara Gas was attacked in the same waterway; one Indian seafarer from that vessel remains missing.

A Liberia-flagged tanker carrying three Indian seafarers has been hit by a projectile near the Strait of Hormuz — and the first official accounts of what happened to its crew do not agree. India's government says everyone on board is safe. The vessel's operator says one crew member is missing and 11 were injured.

What India says

Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal said the MT Navig8 Messi was targeted on November 18 while approaching the Strait of Hormuz. "All 3 Indian nationals, along with the entire crew, are safe and accounted for, with no serious injuries reported," he said in a post on X. "One Indian officer has been shifted to a hospital for first-aid treatment and medical evaluation." Sonowal said the government is in close contact with the ship management company and is continuously tracking developments.

What the operator says

ADNOC Logistics & Services, whose group majority-owns the Navig8 fleet, confirmed that one of its tankers was attacked on the evening of November 17 while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Seatrade Maritime. The company said one seafarer was missing, search and rescue operations were ongoing, the remaining crew had been evacuated, and 11 crew members had sustained injuries and were receiving medical care. Maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the vessel as the Liberian-flagged product tanker Navig8 Messi, struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman; the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency likewise reported a tanker hit near that position, a fire on board extinguished, and one crew member missing.

The accounts cannot both be complete. They differ on the date (the evening of November 17 versus November 18), on whether anyone is missing, and on the number injured. The nationality of the crew member reported missing by the operator has not been established, and no source has established who fired the projectile. Seatrade Maritime reported this was the second reported attack on the Navig8 Messi in the strait, that the vessel has appeared on Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority blacklist of "non-compliant" vessels since August, and that the incident is the 18th confirmed attack on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz so far in November.

The second attack in two days

On November 16, the Panama-flagged LPG tanker MT Tara Gas, carrying 24 Indian seafarers, was struck in the Strait of Hormuz. India's Ministry of External Affairs said 21 Indian crew members were evacuated ashore at Khasab in Oman, two injured crew members were admitted to hospital, and one Indian seafarer remained missing, with the Indian Embassy in Oman monitoring the search. We covered that attack, and the search for the missing seafarer, in our earlier report.

What to watch

The Strait of Hormuz carries a substantial share of the world's petroleum shipments, and the November attacks have made it the most dangerous waterway for the Indian seafarers who crew a large share of the world's merchant fleet. For the families of the Navig8 Messi's crew, the open question is which account is right. India's shipping ministry says it is tracking the situation continuously through the ship's managers; the operator says a search is still under way. Until one side's figures are confirmed by the other, the casualty toll from this attack should be treated as unresolved.
